extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent Office primary examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/patent attorneys) evaluating or submitting 37 CFR 1.131/1.132 affidavits or declarations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating the sufficiency, timeliness, and probative value of affidavits/declarations submitted under 37 CFR 1.131 (antedating references) and 1.132 (traversing rejections), and the proper handling by examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient to show (antedating reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit/declaration must be sufficient to show one of: (A) reduction to practice of the invention prior to the effective date of the reference; or (B) conception of the invention prior to the effective date of the reference coupled with due diligence from prior to the reference date to a subsequent (actual) reduction to practice; or (C) conception of the invention prior to the effective date of the reference coupled with due diligence from prior to the reference date to the filing date of the application (constructive reduction to practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the alternative bases for antedating a reference under 37 CFR 1.131. Conception alone is insufficient unless followed by reasonable diligence demonstrated by other acts (actual reduction or filing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception must be definite and provable
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is the mental part of the inventive act, but it must be capable of proof, as by drawings, complete disclosure to another person, etc.; conception is more than a mere vague idea and must comprehend the means themselves and their interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception requires evidence (disclosure, drawings, model) showing the inventor formed a complete and definite idea of the invention such that one skilled in the art could understand it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof of actual reduction to practice requires a showing that the apparatus actually existed and worked for its intended purpose. For some simple devices, mere construction, photographs, articles and technical reports describing the device in detail may be sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should assess whether submitted exhibits (photographs, reports, articles, constructions) demonstrate actual existence and operative utility; simplicity of device may reduce the needed evidentiary burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 131 affidavit purpose and relation to interference law
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of filing a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit is to antedate the effective date of a reference; though sufficiency parallels interference priority standards, Rule 131 practice is not strictly controlled by interference law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception and reduction-to-practice required under Rule 131 need not be identical to interference definitions; notably, Rule 131 affidavits/declarations do not require corroboration and may rely on the applicant's own affidavit. Proof of utility is required only if the reference discloses a utility; whether test results are needed depends on the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence must be evidenced (binary standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where conception occurs prior to the date of the reference but reduction to practice is afterward, an applicant must show evidence of facts establishing diligence. In patent law an inventor is either diligent or not; there are no degrees of diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence is judged on the particular facts; the record must set forth explanations for inactivity (courts/USPTO will not speculate). Diligence is material only if prior conception is clearly established. The critical period begins just prior to the effective date of the reference and ends with actual or constructive reduction to practice; only diligence before reduction to practice matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony in interference sometimes substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: In place of an affidavit or declaration, the testimony of the applicant in an interference may sometimes be used to antedate a reference in lieu of a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit or declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used, the part of the testimony forming the basis for priority over the reference should be specifically pointed out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic limits on acts relied upon (35 U.S.C. 104)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts relied upon to establish a date of invention must have been carried out in this country or in a NAFTA country or a WTO member country; the 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit/declaration must contain an allegation to that effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective-date limitations apply: dates of completion in NAFTA/WTO countries may only be established on or after statutory effective dates (e.g., Dec. 8, 1993 for NAFTA). If information in such countries is not available to the same extent as in the U.S., appropriate inferences or other statutory actions may be taken to aid the requesting party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibits disposition and compliance (37 CFR 1.91)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibits filed as part of an affidavit/declaration must comply with the requirements of 37 CFR 1.91 to be entered into an application file; exhibits not complying may be disposed of or returned at the Office's discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should check exhibit compliance with 1.91; see MPEP § 608.03(a) for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary examiner review and review routes
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficiency of affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 should be reviewed and decided by a primary examiner. Review of formal sufficiency/propriety is by petition to Technology Center Directors; merits review is by appeal to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions of timeliness/refusal to enter are reviewable by petition (not appeal) in certain circumstances; see MPEP § 715.08 and applicable appeal/petition paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonable presentation / Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 must be timely presented to be admitted. They are timely if submitted: (A) prior to a final rejection; (B) before appeal in an application not having a final rejection; or (C) after final rejection when submitted (1) with a first reply after final rejection to overcome a new ground/requirement in the final rejection, or (2) with a satisfactory showing under 37 CFR 1.116(b) or 1.195, or (3) under 37 CFR 1.129(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All admitted affidavits/declarations must be acknowledged and commented upon in the examiner's next action. Affidavits filed after appeal are governed by 37 CFR 1.195 and MPEP § 1211.02. Review of refusal to enter as untimely is by petition, not appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review for prior public use/on sale and best mode issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits/declarations and accompanying evidence must be reviewed to determine whether they show that the claimed invention was in public use or on sale in this country more than one year prior to the effective filing date (statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)). When the evidence relies on an embodiment not disclosed in the application, the best mode requirement must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an affidavit overcomes a rejection, prior public use/on-sale activities may still create an unovercome statutory bar. A best mode rejection should only be made if the record, as a whole, establishes by a preponderance that the specification fails to set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.132 — affidavits/declarations traversing rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary examiner is responsible to review and decide whether 1.132 submissions are responsive and present sufficient facts to overcome the rejection. This rule serves as general policy for affidavit evidence traversing rejections not covered by other specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.65 (effective to withdraw rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Template: 'The [affidavit/declaration] under 37 CFR 1.132 filed [date] is sufficient to overcome the rejection of claim [#] based upon [statutory grounds].'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert proper bracketed items (affidavit/declaration, filing date, claim numbers, the rejection/statutory grounds). Use when evidence is sufficient to withdraw rejection; follow guidance in MPEP § 716.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.66 (insufficient to overcome rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Template: 'The [affidavit/declaration] under 37 CFR 1.132 filed [date] is insufficient to overcome the rejection of claim [#] based upon [statutory grounds] as set forth in the last Office action because:' followed by specific reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the template, set forth detailed reasons for insufficiency (e.g., untimely, fails to set forth facts, facts not germane, not commensurate with claim scope). Include detailed explanation and appropriate sub-form paragraphs (7.66.01–7.66.05) as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.66.01 — Affiant has never seen invention (insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit includes statements amounting to an affirmation that the affiant has never seen the claimed subject matter before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statements are not relevant to nonobviousness and provide no objective evidence; use this form paragraph with full explanation as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.66.02 — Invention works as intended (insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit states that the claimed subject matter functions as intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not relevant to the issue of nonobviousness and provides no objective evidence of nonobviousness; include detailed explanation when using this paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.66.03 — Refers only to invention, not claims (insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit refers only to the system described in an application and not to the individual claims, failing to show that objective evidence is commensurate in scope with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An affidavit must tie objective evidence to the claim scope; if it does not, it is insufficient. Provide full explanation when invoking this reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.66.04 — No evidence of long‑felt need (insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit asserts the claimed subject matter solved a long‑standing problem but provides no showing that others of ordinary skill were working on the problem or would have been unable to solve it given the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of corroborating evidence about others working on the problem or the continued inability to solve it renders this assertion weak; provide detailed explanation as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.66.05 — Conclusion that rebuttal evidence fails
rubrics_metrics.description: A concluding form paragraph asserting that, when all evidence is considered, the totality of rebuttal evidence fails to outweigh the evidence of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should be presented as a conclusion to the insufficiency explanation and must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 with supporting detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally applicable criterion — Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence traversing rejections must be timely or seasonably filed to be entered and entitled to consideration. (Timeliness conditions mirror the 1.131 timing rules.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely if (1) prior to final rejection; (2) before appeal in an application not having a final rejection; or (3) after final rejection when submitted with first reply to overcome a new ground, or with satisfactory showing under 1.116(b)/1.195, or under 1.129(a). See cases (e.g., In re Rothermel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally applicable criterion — Consideration of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence traversing rejections must be considered by the examiner whenever present; all entered affidavits/declarations must be acknowledged and commented upon in the next action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extent of commentary depends on action taken: if evidence overcomes the prima facie case, comments should align with statements of reasons for allowance; if insufficient, examiner must specifically explain why (general statements without support are insufficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence of nonobviousness must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits/declarations containing objective evidence (criticality, unexpected results, commercial success, long‑felt need, failure of others, skepticism of experts, etc.) must be considered when present in evaluating obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations must always be considered en route to a determination of obviousness; comparative data in the specification should be considered. Lack of objective evidence does not weigh for obviousness, but failure to rebut a prima facie case can be dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement for secondary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Any secondary evidence must be related to the claimed invention to be probative — a factual and legal nexus is required between the objective evidence and the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must determine whether the evidence of secondary considerations has a sufficient nexus to the merits of the claimed invention to be given substantial weight (see case law cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probative value — objective evidence must be supported by proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence (unexpected results, commercial success, long‑felt need, inoperability of prior art, invention before reference, derivation allegations) must be factually supported by appropriate affidavits/declarations to be probative; attorney arguments cannot substitute for evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual evidence preferred to opinion; expert opinion may be considered if not addressing the ultimate legal conclusion and is supported by factual basis. Examiner must assess expert interest, opposing evidence, and factual support when weighing opinions. Conclusory statements without support have little weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing objective evidence against prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining patentability, evidence supporting patentability must be weighed against evidence supporting the examiner's prima facie case; the ultimate determination is by preponderance of the whole record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence should be evaluated along with the facts on which the prima facie case rests; all competent rebuttal evidence taken as a whole is weighed against the prima facie evidence. If examiner remains unconvinced, the next action must identify reasons (e.g., commercial success not convincing or not related). See MPEP § 2144.08 and case law for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegations of unexpected results — substantial proof required
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between the claimed invention and prior art may be expected to result in property differences; the issue is whether properties differ to such an extent that the difference is unexpected (difference in kind rather than degree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater‑than‑expected results (including synergism or greater‑than‑additive effects) can be evidence of nonobviousness, but applicant must show that results exceed those expected from the prior art to an unobvious extent and provide practical advantage. Comparative tests/data are often required; mere assertions are insufficient.
